When a College President requests and authorizes CUNY Peace Officers to be armed, storage of the firearms will be at the respective college location designated by the University Director of Public Safety. In the case of Special Public Safety units providing University-wide law enforcement services (i.e. S.A.F.E. Teams) wherein said officers may also constitute part of the individual college Peace Officer security force, firearms may be stored either at the college with the approval of the College President or at University Director of Public Safety office.

CUNY Peace Officers authorized to bear firearms receive additional compensation, (currently $1,791 per annum), upon successfully completing the New York State certified training and being duly licensed by the NYPD. CUNY Peace Officer shall also undergo an additional background investigation before being licensed to carry a firearm. If the request and authorization to receive firearms training and certification are made by a college president, the additional compensation is paid by the requesting college administration. However, costs associated with the arming of any CUNY Peace Officer i.e. firearms, holsters, ammunition, gun lockers, training licensing and background investigations are borne by the Central Office (The University Director of Public Safety).
POSSESSION OF FIREARMS WHILE OFF DUTY
CUNY Peace Officers are not authorized to carry firearms while off-duty.

CARRY 1. When carrying a firearm, Campus Peace Officer shall carry the firearm in a manner which will not allow access by an unauthorized person. A firearm must be carried in an appropriate holster that is in good working order, and that is specially designed for the firearm being carried in order to afford maximum protection against loss of the firearm. Firearms may not be carried in a briefcase, handbag, fanny pack, hip pack, tote bag, knapsack, paper bag or similar device.
When firearm is carried in the course of official duty, firearm is to be fully loaded with appropriate ammunition. If the firearm is semi-automatic, it shall be chamber loaded with a full magazine.
The firearm shall not be drawn, exposed or displayed in an inappropriate manor not in the furtherance of the Peace Officer duties to protect, safeguard and secure the CUNY campuses.

CUNY Peace Officers shall be subject to disciplinary action in accordance with the applicable collective bargaining agreement, in the event a firearm is drawn, exposed or displayed in an inappropriate manor – not in furtherance of their Peace Officer duties to protect, safeguard and secure the CUNY campuses.

PROHIBITED TO CARRY 1. Peace Officers shall not be in possession of a firearm if they are, or if there is any possibility that they may become, unfit for duty because of the consumption of intoxicants. 2. A Campus Peace Officer who reasonably believes another Campus Peace Officer may be unfit for duty in violation of Section I.B.1. shall immediately inform a supervisor and record his or her observations in writing. 3. The supervisor shall immediately take appropriate steps to address the allegation including: conducting an investigation of the allegation, if the supervisor is responsible for conducting such internal investigations, to determine whether the Campus Peace Officer is or was in violation of this section in light of all credible relevant information; and/or immediately notifying the College Public Safety Director, and immediately notifying the Police Department's License Division Incident Section of the alleged violation. 4. In conducting an investigation of the allegation, credible relevant information may include: statements of the Campus Peace Officer at issue, other employees, or other witnesses; any Breathalyzer or other test results available; the supervisor's own observations; and the time elapsed since the alleged misconduct. 5. If a supervisor or other investigating entity determines that the Campus Peace Officer is currently unfit for duty, or that the Campus Peace Officer has violated these guidelines, then the Campus Peace Officer's firearm privileges shall be suspended and firearms and ammunition seized according to the procedure in section [XII – E&F]. 6. Any Campus Peace Officer who is or has been found to be in violation of this section, whether or not firearm privileges are suspended, may be subject to disciplinary action in accordance with the applicable collective
bargaining agreement, and/or referral to counseling services or to other health care providers. The Campus Peace Officer may also contact such counseling services or health care providers directly.

If a Campus Peace Officer receives psychiatric treatment or treatment for alcoholism or drug abuse, or is subject to any disability or condition that may affect the ability to safely possess or use a firearm, the Campus Peace Officer is required to notify The College Public Safety Director immediately. The Campus Peace Officer must also immediately notify Police Department's License Division Incident Section of the treatment, disability or condition. The employee may be required to surrender his/her firearm until s/he is found to be fit for duty, after appropriate investigation by the agency. (See Revocation of Firearm Privileges.)

STORAGE 1. If a firearm is not being carried, it must be properly secured in a manner that minimizes the risk that an unauthorized person may readily obtain it. New York City Administrative Code Section 10-312 makes it a criminal violation for any person who is the lawful owner or lawful custodian of a firearm to store or otherwise place or leave such weapon in such a manner or under such circumstances that it is out of his or her immediate possession or control, without having rendered the weapon inoperable by employing a safety locking device, such as a trigger lock, a combination handle, or a gunlock. 2. Firearms must be safeguarded at all times and may not be left in an unattended motor vehicle, desk drawer, locker or filing cabinet, other than a locker provided for that purpose in a secured CUNY college facility. In the event that the firearm is not properly safeguarded, as set forth herein, the subject officers may be subject to disciplinary action in accordance with the applicable collective bargaining agreement.

Campus Peace Officers who are hospitalized on an emergency basis shall as soon as practicable notify the agency of their hospital stay so that appropriate arrangements for retrieval and temporary safeguarding of firearms may be made by the college or University Office of Public Safety.
No personal or service firearms shall be carried by a Campus Peace Officer during off-duty employment unless written request has been granted by The

University Director of Public Safety or designee. The University Director of Public Safety or designee will provide authorization in a written memorandum to the requesting campus Peace Officer. A copy of this memorandum will be forwarded to the Chancellor, Executive Vice Chancellor and Chief Operating Officer and the Special Counsel to the Chancellor, prior to any authorization.
In no event shall a Campus Peace Officer licensed by the New York City Police Department carry a firearm during such off-duty employment unless the terms of the license authorize such use.

The University Director of Public Safety or designee shall determine that the employee engaging in off-duty employment has obtained any license necessary to the performance of the off-duty function, such as security guard, firearms dealer, or gunsmith, as a condition of granting authorization.

The University Director of Public Safety or designee shall determine that the use of the firearm for the purpose of off-duty employment does not conflict with the interests of the agency or of the City and does not violate the applicable conflicts of interest laws and policies, as a condition of granting authorization.

Any Campus Peace Officer who loses either a service or personal firearm either through theft or other circumstances, whether inside or outside New York City, shall immediately report said incident to the law enforcement authority having jurisdiction over the geographic location where the loss occurred. After notifying the Local Law Enforcement Authority, said Campus Peace Officer shall immediately report the loss to his/her Director of Public Safety and The University Director of Public Safety or designee. The agency shall notify the Local Law enforcement Authority to verify the reporting of such incident. The Campus Peace Officer must also immediately notify the Police Department's License Division Incident Section of the loss or theft. Thereafter an investigation is conducted by The University Director of Public Safety and, if applicable, by the Police Department and/or the License Division.

Any Campus Peace Officer who, while on or off-duty, publicly displays or uses an un-holstered firearm other than at an authorized small arms/shooting range shall report the incident immediately to his/her Public Safety Director and The University Director of Public Safety or designee, and complete an incident report. The CUNY University Director of Public Safety shall immediately notify the Local Law Enforcement Authority having jurisdiction over the geographic location where the incident occurred. The CUNY University Director of Public Safety or designee must also immediately notify the Police Department’s License Division Incident Section of the incident. Thereafter, an investigation shall be conducted by The University Director of Public Safety and, if applicable, by the Police Department and/or the License Division.

The agency may confiscate the firearm pending a full investigation. If the investigation determines that the subject officer engaged in an improper use of the firearm, the subject officer may be subject to disciplinary action in accordance with the applicable collective bargaining agreement.
SUSPENSION AND REVOCATION OF FIREARM PRIVILEGES

The University Office of Public Safety shall maintain standardized policies on the suspension, revocation, and restoration of firearm privileges resulting from Campus Peace Officer conduct including disciplinary, criminal, medical, psychological or other circumstances or incidents which affect the ability to possess a firearm.
The following circumstances may result in the suspension and/or revocation of firearm privileges, which include but are not limited to:
Improper discharge or public display of un-holstered firearm;
Disciplinary action resulting in a finding of misconduct;
Receipt of psychiatric treatment or treatment for alcoholism or drug abuse or the presence of any disability or other condition that may affect the ability to safely possess or use a firearm;
Failure to properly safeguard a firearm, including loss, theft, improper handling, or failure to utilize required safety locking device;
Arrest, indictment, or conviction, inclusive of a desk appearance ticket and of a summons other than a traffic infraction;
Acts of domestic violence resulting in a conviction or plea of guilty or nolo contendere;

Campus Peace Officer becomes the subject or recipient of an order of protection, including a temporary order of protection, or an order of suspension or ineligibility under Criminal Procedure Law § 530.14 or Family Court Act § 842-a;
Loss or theft of firearms license;
Alteration, mutilation or destruction of a firearms license; or

Whenever CUNY Public Safety Department determines that a Campus Peace Officer is unfit to possess a firearm, the Campus Peace Officer’s firearms privileges shall be revoked. A report indicating the grounds for the determination shall be given to the Campus Peace Officer (who shall be requested to sign and date acknowledging receipt of such report). The report shall be placed in the employee’s personnel file; and, in the case of a Campus Peace Officer who has a firearms license, rifle and shotgun permit, and/or Special Patrolman status from the Police Department, sent to the Police Department License Division.
Whenever a Campus Peace Officer has his/her firearm privileges revoked for any reason:

All firearms, including personal firearms and rifles and shotguns, ammunition, shield and identification card shall be surrendered by the Campus Peace Officer immediately and shall be secured by CUNY Public Safety. If the agency does not have the capacity to secure the weapons appropriately, the weapons and ammunition shall be vouchered for safekeeping at the local police precinct. CUNY Public Safety Department shall conduct an investigation to determine that all firearms, rifles, shotguns and ammunition have been seized, and CUNY Public Safety records of firearms and ammunition purchases shall be checked. CUNY

Public Safety shall if necessary arrange for the retrieval of firearms, rifles, shotguns and ammunition not surrendered. A written record shall be kept of all firearms, rifles, shotguns and ammunition received.

The Campus Peace Officer shall be given a written order notifying that his or her privileges have been revoked, reiterating the surrender requirement, and directing him/her to report for issuance of a new identification card. The new card shall clearly indicate that the Campus Peace Officer is not entitled to use or purchase firearms, rifles or shotguns. The employee shall be required to sign and date an acknowledgement of receipt.

Notwithstanding the provisions of paragraphs 1 and 2 above, CUNY may waive the requirement that the identification card be surrendered if the identification card does not confer unlimited peace officer status, and thus the ability to purchase a firearm, rifle, shotgun or ammunition without a license or permit, upon the campus Peace Officer.

The Police Department License Division shall be notified of the revocation if the Campus Peace Officer has a firearms license, rifle and shotgun permit, and/or Special Patrolman status from the Police Department.

The firearms privileges of a Campus Peace Officer may be temporarily suspended pending investigation and final decision in a case of alleged unfitness for duty (as described in Section XII.B.1 above) or if it appears that one of the grounds for revocation in Section XII B. above exists and that suspension is appropriate under the circumstances, or if a Campus Peace Officer’s license to possess a firearm or permit to possess a rifle or shotgun has been suspended by the Police Department’s License Division.
When a Campus Peace Officer’s firearms privileges are suspended:

The Campus Peace Officer must surrender all firearms, rifles, shotguns, ammunition, ID card and shield. The supervisor effecting the suspension shall question the Campus Peace Officer regarding the number and location of firearms, rifles and shotguns possessed and shall if necessary arrange for the retrieval of firearms not present at the scene. The surrender requirement shall be reiterated in writing as soon as practicable. All items shall be stored at a designated CUNY Public Safety Department facility or with the Police Department and an NYPD property voucher or other record kept.
The Campus Peace Officer may also be suspended or placed on modified duty in accordance with the applicable collective bargaining agreement.

The supervisor shall make a complete written report, including copies of all available evidence, to the agency head or designee and to the direct supervisor of the employee in question, with a copy kept in the employee’s personnel file.

The Campus Peace Officer shall be given a written order noting that his or her firearms privileges have been suspended, reiterating the surrender requirement, and directing him/her to report for issuance of a new identification card. The new card shall clearly indicate that the employee is not entitled to purchase firearms, rifles or shotguns. The Campus Peace Officer shall be required to sign and date an acknowledgement of receipt.

Notwithstanding the provisions of paragraphs 1 and 4 above, CUNY Public Safety may waive the requirement that the identification card be surrendered if the identification card does not confer unlimited peace officer status, and thus the ability to purchase a firearm, rifle, shotgun or ammunition without a license or permit, upon the campus Peace Officer.

The Police Department License Division shall be notified of the suspension if the Campus Peace Officer has a firearms license, rifle and shotgun permit, and/or Special Patrolman status from the Police Department.

Whenever a Campus Peace Officer voluntarily surrenders a service firearm for safekeeping due to vacation, hospitalization, or other similar circumstances, the agency shall interview the employee in order to ascertain the reason the employee is surrendering the firearm, so that a determination may be made whether the voluntary surrender may indicate the presence of a disability or condition which may affect the ability to safely possess or use a firearm.

If for any reason, the supervisor conducting the interview determines there exists an underlying reason predicating the surrender of the firearm which may indicate the presence of a disability or condition which may affect the ability to safely possess or use a firearm, The University Director of Public Safety or designee must be notified and advised of the circumstances and if appropriate, shall order
an investigation and/or a referral for agency counseling services and/or to other health care providers deemed appropriate.

If the Department determines that there is an underlying reason predicating the surrender of the firearm which may indicate the presence of a disability or condition which may affect the ability to safely possess or use a firearm, the agency may suspend or revoke the Campus Peace Officer’s firearm privileges pursuant to the provisions of Section XII.

Prior to the return of a firearm voluntarily surrendered by a campus Peace Officer, The University Office of Public Safety shall interview the Campus Peace Officer to determine whether the Campus Peace Officer remains fit to possess a firearm, and is not subject to any of the conditions or circumstances listed in Section XII.B. The return of the firearm may be delayed pending further investigation.

Campus Peace Officer shall not be eligible for the restoration of their firearm privileges unless: 1. All charges against the Campus Peace Officer that were related to the revocation of the privileges have been adjudicated and the Campus Peace Officer is not on probation for an offense/incident which led to the revocation of the privilege or subject to any of the conditions or circumstances listed in Section XII. 2. Any Campus Peace Officer requesting to have his/her firearm privileges restored shall submit documentation and evidence relevant to the grounds of the revocation, which may include: a) Copy of the Police Department’s complaint/arrest report;
Copy of desk appearance ticket or summons;
Certificate of disposition from the concerned court; or

Upon receipt of such a request: 1. The request shall be forwarded to the officer’s immediate supervisor or other designated responsible party within the CUNY Public Safety Department, who shall investigate and review the request and make a written recommendation as to whether the request shall be granted or

denied and specify reasons. In the course of the investigation and review the responsible party may confer as appropriate with other agency employees including medical, legal and operational personnel. The request and recommendation shall then be forwarded through channels to the University of Public Safety or designee.

The University Director of Public Safety or designee, in consultation with respective College President and/or Executive Vice Chancellor and Chief Operating Officer shall review all factors and circumstances and determine whether the firearms should be restored. The request with all attachments and a written order noting the final determination and its grounds, including copies of all documents considered, shall be retained in the Campus Peace Officer’s personnel file.
CUNY Public Safety Department may order a Campus Peace Officer to undergo an independent medical and/or psychological examination before restoring a firearm.

Before any firearm or ammunition is returned to a Campus Peace Officer who has a firearms license CUNY Public Safety Department, shall confirm the employee’s status with the Police Department’s License Division and determine whether the Campus Peace Officer is under investigation or has had his or her license or permit suspended or revoked.

Once approval is granted and subject to any necessary re-qualification by the campus Peace Officer, the Campus Peace Officer’s firearm, ammunition, and shield will be inspected and returned, and the Campus Peace Officer may receive an updated identification card. The officer will be required to sign a receipt for the items received.

Campus Peace Officers who are authorized to carry a firearm must pass a firearm qualification course annually, for every firearm they are authorized to use in the course of their employment. Should a Campus Peace Officer fail to qualify, his/her firearms will remain with the University Office of Public Safety gun custodian until such time as the Campus Peace Officer receives additional training and is able to qualify.
PERMITTED FIREARMS AND MAINTENANCE OF FIREARMS
Only approved firearms and ammunition may be possessed by Campus Peace Officers.
Campus Peace Officers must properly clean and maintain their firearm. When cleaning the firearm, it must be unloaded with the muzzle pointed in a safe direction.

Campus Peace Officer will be subject to inspections of every firearm they are authorized to use in the course of their employment at least once a year or otherwise directed by the University Office of Public Safety.

Campus Peace Officers will notify the University Office of Public Safety to schedule an inspection whenever a service firearm appears to be defective. If on inspection a service firearm is determined to be defective, the Campus Peace Officer shall be given a notice and an acknowledgment of receipt for the firearm.

The University Office of Public Safety shall repair the service firearm or make arrangements to have the firearm repaired. In this case a receipt shall be given to the campus Peace Officer, with copies for his/her supervisor and personnel file.
COMMUNICATION WITH NEW YORK CITY POLICE DEPARTMENT

The University Director of Public Safety or gun custodian is designated as the point of contact with the New York City Police Department for all information relevant to whether and under what circumstances a Campus Peace Officer should have the privilege of carrying firearms. In his/her absence these matters will be referred to the Executive Vice Chancellor and Chief Operating Officer or designee.

CUNY’s gun custodian shall forward to The University Director of Public Safety or designee any information that may be helpful in a determination regarding suspension, revocation, or restoration of firearm privileges.
All Campus Peace Officers who are authorized by CUNY to obtain firearms license(s) in the regular course of their duties shall required to obtain a firearms
license for such activity from the New York City Police Department, notwithstanding whether the Campus Peace Officer is otherwise authorized or licensed to carry a firearm.

If a Campus Peace Officer has a firearms license, rifle and shotgun permit and/or Special Patrolman status from the Police Department, then the gun custodian and/or the Campus Peace Officer shall immediately inform the Police Department's License Division Incident Section as well as the precinct of occurrence (or the relevant Local Law enforcement Authority if the incident occurs outside New York City) upon the occurrence of the following incidents or circumstances: 1. Discharge or public display of un-holstered firearm other than at an authorized small arms/shooting range;
Failure to properly safeguard, including loss, theft, improper handling, or failure to utilize required safety locking device;
Loss or theft of firearms license, identification card, or shield; or

If a Campus Peace Officer has a firearms license, rifle and shotgun permit and/or Special Patrolman status from the Police Department, then the gun custodian and the Campus Peace Officer shall immediately inform the Police Department's License Division Incident Section upon the occurrence of the following incidents or circumstances:
Arrest, indictment, or conviction, inclusive of a desk appearance ticket and of a summons other than a traffic infraction;
Acts of domestic violence that result in a conviction or a plea of guilty or nolo contendere;

Campus Peace Officer becomes the subject or recipient of an order of protection, including a temporary order of protection, or an order of suspension or ineligibility under Criminal Procedure Law § 530.14 or family Court Act § 842-a;
Receipt of psychiatric treatment or treatment for alcoholism or drug abuse or the presence of any disability or other condition that may affect the ability to safely possess or use a firearm;
Alteration, mutilation or destruction of a firearms license;
Any suspension, revocation, or restoration of firearm privileges;
Any agency seizure or return of firearms and ammunition;
Any voluntary surrender of a firearm or return of a voluntarily surrendered firearm;
Any investigation into whether an employee's firearm privileges should be suspended or revoked and the outcome of any such investigation; or
Any other incident that could result in the revocation of firearm privileges as listed in Section XII.B.

The gun custodian shall inform the Police Department License Division semiannually of the information required by 38 RCNY 5-24(a)(3)(iii), including the names, badge/tax numbers, and identifying information of all Campus Peace Officer who are licensed to possess the firearm by the NYPD.
Reports under this section to the NYPD and to any other agency or division requested by the Police Department shall be by phone with follow up fax.

inst.title: Magnetometer [Metal Detector] Policy
b: This instruction prescribes The City University of New York Public Safety Department policy regarding the use of magnetometers (metal detectors) as set forth by the University Director of Public Safety for the effective administration of campus public safety operations and to establish guidelines for the use of metal detectors.

This policy has been formulated within the scope and intent of the University Public Safety Initiative. Failure to comply with these policies, instructions and guidelines may result in a recommendation to appropriate college officials that disciplinary charges be filed.

It is the policy of The City University of New York Public Safety Department to equip each constituent college with at least one University-approved magnetometer for use during special events where the college president or his designee deems metal detection a prudent operational procedure. There is no University mandate to employ metal detectors. They are provided to the colleges as an added public safety resource. The decision to utilize metal detectors is made when there is a safety concern regarding the potential illegal possession or use of firearms or other deadly weapons on college property.

When a college makes the decision to use a metal detector, at least one armed CUNY Peace Officer must be in the immediate vicinity of the screening operation. Metal detection screening operations shall not be conducted without an armed CUNY Public Safety Peace Officer or other armed sworn law enforcement /police officer being present. Alternatively a college may establish a protocol with the NYC Police Department or other appropriate law enforcement agency whereby an officer of the law enforcement entity will respond to the screening site in less than five minutes pursuant to a request from the college. In general, college arrangements in connection with the use of magnetometers should seek to minimize officer response time, thereby enhancing campus safety.

It is the policy of The City University of New York Public Safety Department, to confiscate illegal firearms or other deadly weapons and individuals found to be in possession of illegal firearms without appropriate authority or license, will be arrested. These weapons must be vouchered in accordance with established NYPD arrest procedures.

The purpose of this policy is to prevent weapons from entering colleges and /or any CUNY facilities, while ensuring the safety of Peace Officers, the college community and the public who may be in the vicinity of the screening process during a potential arrest situation involving the illegal possession of firearms or other deadly weapons.

When a metal detector search is being conducted, signs must be posted outside the building at every entrance in order to provide notice to all persons entering the college that they will be required to submit to a weapons screening as a condition of entry. (See attached notice)

All persons who wish to enter the building will be searched. Under no circumstances may particular individuals be singled out for search, unless there is probable cause to believe that the individual is in possession of a weapon.
When hand-held metal detection wands are utilized, only female officers will scan female individuals and only male officers will scan male individuals.

Prior to scanning, the Peace Officer will request individuals to place bags or parcels which they are carrying onto a table and to remove any metal objects from their pockets or person and lay these items on a tray.
Persons who refuse to cooperate will be advised that they need not submit to a scan but that failure to do so will result in denial of entry.
Pregnant women shall be advised that they may request a pat down search by a female officer in lieu of a scan.

If the metal detector activates while scanning a bag or parcel, its owner will be requested to open the bag or parcel. If the owner does not wish to open the bag or parcel, he/she may refuse to do so, but will be advised that such refusal will result in denial of entry.

During the initial scanning process, CUNY Peace Officers should make every effort to avoid personal contact and ensure that the scanning equipment does not come into physical contact with the individual being scanned.

If the metal detector activates and the source of the alarm is not apparent (e.g., belt, jewelry), the CUNY Peace Officer conducting the scan will direct the individual to remove any remaining metal objects from his/her person and will conduct a second scan. If the detector activates again, the individual will be advised that if he/she wishes to enter the building, he/she must submit to a hand- held metal detection procedure and to a pat-down. If the individual does not wish to be physically searched, the individual will be advised that he/she must leave the building.
If the individual consents to a search, he/she will be escorted to a private area and will be searched in accordance with the procedures outlined below.
Weapon scanning will proceed in the following manner:
The officer will stand to the left side of the individual to be scanned. Scanning will begin at the left chest area and proceed down to the feet.
The officer will move to the rear of the individual and scan the left side from the feet to the head.
The officer will then scan the back of the individual from the head to the feet.
As the officer moves to the right side, the officer will scan the individual from the feet to the head.
The officer will then scan the individual’s right side from the right chest to the feet.
The officer will scan all parcels and/or bags.
Prior to conducting the search, the officer will once again advise the individual that he/she need not submit to the search but that such refusal will result in denial of entry.
If the individual agrees to be searched, the officer will again ask him/her to remove any remaining metal objects from his/her person.
Only male officers will search male individuals. Only Female officers will search female individuals only.

The search shall be conducted only in the area of the body which activated the metal detector. The search shall commence with the patting of the individual’s external clothing in the vicinity of pockets, belts, shoulders or other specific areas, for the limited purpose of discovering items which may have activated the metal detecting device.

If the officer conducting the search feels an object which he/she believes may have activated the metal detecting device, the officer shall ask the individual to remove the object. If the person refuses to remove the object, the officer shall remove it.

If the object voluntarily provided by the individual or removed from the individual could have activated the metal detector, the search must cease. The Peace Officer will then scan the individual again, and the search will be continued only if the metal detector is again activated during the scan of that individual.
Under no circumstances will a strip search or body cavity search be conducted by any member of the CUNY Public Safety Department.
If the metal detector is again activated and all options short of a strip search or body cavity search have been exhausted, the person shall be denied entry.

When an individual is found to be in possession of contraband (e.g. weapons, controlled substance), CUNY Peace Officers will effect an arrest. When an arrest is made, the Peace Officer will take custody of the contraband and voucher all items at the local police precinct according to New York City Police Department guidelines.
All removed personal property which is not contraband or prohibited by college rules or regulations, must be returned to that individual upon completion of the search.

IMPORTANT NOTE: A college need not have armed officers or firearms assigned to its campus to comply with this Operation Instruction. At the request of the college, a state certified and trained armed CUNY Peace Officer will be provided by the Office of the University Director of Public Safety for magnetometer operations. Officers assigned to magnetometer operations in an armed capacity who do not carry firearms at their colleges as a matter of policy, will be issued their assigned firearm at the Office of the University Director of Public Safety prior to the commencement of magnetometer operations. Officers will return said firearms to the Office of the University Director of Public Safety upon completion of the screening process. If the completion of said assignment is during off hours, weekends or holidays, officers are to safeguard their service firearms and return them to the Office of the University Director of Public Safety on the next business day at 0900 hours. Under no circumstances are firearms to be used by officers at the college during normal patrol operations unless specifically authorized to do so by the College President. At the request of the college, the armed CUNY Peace Officer may be in uniform or plainclothes, in which case the officer’s firearm will be concealed. Alternatively, a college may establish a protocol with the NYC Police Department or other appropriate law enforcement agency whereby an officer of the law enforcement entity will respond to the screening site in less than five minutes pursuant to a request from the college. In general, college arrangements in connection with the use of magnetometers should seek to minimize officer response time, thereby enhancing campus safety.

NOTICE WEAPONS ARE NOT PERMITTED IN ANY CITY UNIVERSITY OF NEW YORK BUILDING. PERSONS WISHING TO ENTER CUNY COLLEGE BUILDINGS OR PROPERTY MAY BE REQUIRED TO SUBMIT TO A METAL DETECTOR SCAN BY CUNY PEACE OFFICERS. DEPENDING ON THE INITIAL SCAN, A PATDOWN OR MORE INTRUSIVE PERSONAL SEARCH MAY BE NECESSARY TO ENSURE THAT WEAPONS ARE NOT BROUGHT ONTO CUNY PROPERTY. BAGS AND PARCELS MAY ALSO BE SEARCHED BY MEANS OF METAL DETECTING DEVICES, BY HAND, OR OTHERWISE. PERSONS WHO DO NOT WISH TO BE SEARCHED OR TO HAVE BAGS OR PARCELS SEARCHED ARE FREE TO LEAVE AND WILL BE DENIED ENTRY. TO AVOID DAMAGE, FLOPPY DISKS, COMPUTER DISKS, AND CASSETTE TAPES SHOULD BE REMOVED PRIOR TO SCANNING. PERSONS FOUND TO HAVE IN THEIR POSSESSION UNLAWFUL OR UNLICENSED WEAPONS AT THE TIME OF THE DETECTOR SCAN OR SEARCH WILL BE SUBJECT TO ARREST.
TO: All Directors of Public Safety
FROM: Jose A. Elique, University Director of Security & Public Safety
SUBJECT: Magnetometer (Metal Detector) Policy - SECOND REVISION

COPY: W. Ann Reynolds, Chancellor Laurence F. Mucciolo, Deputy Chancellor Robert E. Diaz, Vice Chancellor for Legal Affairs Brenda Richardson Malone, Vice Chancellor for Faculty & Staff Relations Samuel T. Phillips, University Director of Personnel Vice Presidents and Deans of Administration

As you are aware, the purpose of metal detectors is to reveal the presence of concealed weapons or objects that may be used as weapons. They are provided to the colleges as an added public safety resource.

On a day-to-day basis, metal detectors are generally not employed at the campuses. When the President of a college, in consultation with campus personnel, determines that prudent safety considerations require the use of metal detectors at a particular college event, the protocols set forth in Operations Instruction #21 must be followed. These protocols were developed in consultation with the Office of the University General Counsel.

When the president of the college, or his or her designee, decides to use a metal detector, an armed CUNY Peace Officer (or other armed sworn law enforcement officer) must be within sight and sound of the metal detector screening operation. The officer may be in uniform or plainclothes. The individual screening the public passing through the metal detector may, but need not be a CUNY peace officer. Alternatively a college may establish a protocol with the NYC Police Department or other appropriate law enforcement agency whereby an officer of the law enforcement entity will respond to the screening site in less than five minutes pursuant to a request from the college. In general, college arrangements in connection with the use of magnetometers should seek to minimize officer response time, thereby enhancing campus safety.

The reason an armed peace officer must be in the vicinity of the screening operation is three-fold. First, only a trained law enforcement officer should respond to a situation where it has been determined that an individual has in his possession a deadly weapon. Second, the illegal possession of a firearm or other deadly weapon is a felony in New York State. Anyone found in possession of such a weapon is subject to arrest. Third, weapons must be confiscated and vouchered in accordance with established NYPD arrest procedures. CUNY peace officers are sworn, trained and authorized to make arrests and are familiar with applicable NYPD procedures.

Because campus presidents have typically elected not to arm their peace officers, the Office of the University Director of Public Safety will provide a state certified and trained armed CUNY peace officer to any campus electing to use a magnetometer to enable the campus to comply with Security Instruction #22.
This policy and the accompanying Operations Instruction is effective immediately. JAE:ev Enc Security Instructions\metal-mem\win

inst.title: Use of Police Trained Law Enforcement Canine Patrol
b: To provide for the positive and efficient utilization of The City University of New York (CUNY) Public Safety Department K-9 teams in a manner that will be most effective in attaining CUNY’S goal of serving the University community.
The use of a canine is a recognized tool in attaining the goals of law enforcement in our society. The canine team’s greatest value lies in the deterrent effect of their presence.

All members of the CUNY Public Safety Department must bear in mind that the use of a canine team in making or maintaining an arrest constitutes the use of force or the implied use of force. Therefore, it is imperative that the canine handler be fully cognizant of all the facts and circumstances available surrounding the situation before a decision is made to use a canine for other than deterrent patrol.
Agility Training Training during which the canine must surmount or overcome obstacles, such as walls and tunnels, which are likely to be confronted while working.
Apprehension with Gunfire The ability of the canine to apprehend the “suspect” and not be distracted by gunfire.
Article/Evidence Search A search by the canine to locate various articles or types of evidence within a designated area.
Building Search A search of a structure by the canine in which the dog follows the freshest scent to locate a “suspect” or “subject” hiding in the structure.

Box Search A training exercise, during which the canine enters a field with several boxes, tents, or other objects containing or concealing one or more “suspect” or subject. The canine follows the freshest scent to locate and indicate the hidden suspect (s) or subject (s).
Criminal Apprehension An exercise during which the canine physically apprehends (bites and holds) the “suspect” until the “suspect” is taken into custody (and a release command is issued).
Distance Control The canine is trained to respond to voice commands or hand signals given from a distance by the canine handler.
False Start Should the suspect begin to flee, the canine will remain in a sit position.
Field Search (Marsh Search or Wood Search) A search of a field or other designated area, during which the canine conducts a quarter search of the area to locate and indicate the “suspect” or subject.
Handler Protection The canine is trained to stay in a watch position unless commanded by the canine handler or the canine handler’s safety is threatened.

Law Enforcement Agency Law enforcement agency means any police or peace force, or organization functioning within this state which has by statute or ordinance the responsibility of detecting crime and enforcing the criminal or penal laws of this state.

Law Enforcement Officer Law enforcement officer means any employee of a law enforcement agency, not including a civilian employee, any member of a fire department or force who is assigned to an arson investigation unit pursuant to Public Law 1981, Chapter 409, and any corrections officer or juvenile detention officer.
Off Lead Obedience A series of obedience exercises where the canine is trained to heel alongside the officer and make left, right, and about turns while off lead.
On Lead Obedience A series of obedience exercises where the canine is trained to heel alongside the officer and make left, right, and about turns while on lead.

Recall This exercise shows that the canine handler has complete voice control over the dog in all situations and that the police dog will return to the officer handler, on command, prior to making a physical apprehension.
Scent Work Exercises whereby the canine conducts searches to locate a “suspect,” other subject, evidence or other articles within buildings, other types of interior structures, or exterior areas.

The primary mission of the K-9 Unit is to provide trained canine teams to assist in the prevention and detection of crime, the tracking of persons sought by sworn law enforcement personnel and such other duties as may be directed by competent authority. All members of the service shall cooperate and assist the K-9 Unit in achieving these objectives. The personnel of the K-9 Unit shall perform the regular duties of the K-9 Unit except when their services are required for special details and/or training purposes. The handler’s assignment to the K-9 Unit shall in no manner relieve them from conforming to and complying with other orders of the CUNY Public Safety Department or general provisions of the CUNY Operation Instructions.
REQUESTS FOR USE OF CANINE SERVICE
Use within the City University’s Public Safety Department

Requests for the immediate tactical utilization of the services of the K-9 Unit in accordance with the guidelines of this policy may be made by the president of any college, or his/her designee (i.e. Vice President, College Public Safety Director, Duty Lieutenant, etc.)
Such request shall be made to the Office of the University Director of Public Safety who shall direct that canine assistance be dispatched.

Upon the arrival of the canine handler at the scene, he/she shall be responsible for determining whether or not the circumstances of the incident justify the use of a canine and for determining the tactical utilization of same.

If a supervisory public safety officer is present at the scene, he/she shall assume the responsibility for making the decision on whether or not to deploy the K-9 teams. However, if the handler believes that the use of the canine is unjustified or is tactically unfeasible, he/she will so advise the supervisory public safety officer at the scene who, in fulfilling his/her responsibility, shall comply with the K-9 handler’s recommendation. In every case the handler shall make the final decision on the tactical deployment of the canine if such deployment is authorized by the supervisory officer in charge of the situation.
Use of CUNY K-9 Officers by Outside Law Enforcement Agencies

All requests for dispatch of K-9 Unit personnel for use in areas outside of CUNY property shall be directed to the University Director of Public Safety or his representative. All such requests will be afforded immediate and careful consideration and when, in the opinion of the University public safety official contacted, the services can be provided from the resources available and the need appears to justify the use of a canine, the request shall be approved and the following action taken;

Advise the college public safety official in charge of the K-9 Unit concerning the request, including any special requirements, and if appropriate, direct the dispatch of the K-9 teams which are necessary to meet these requirements.

Advise the requesting agency of the decision concerning their request for special canine support and the approximate time the team(s) from the K-9 Unit will arrive at the designated area to furnish the requested assistance.

The University Director of Public Safety shall verbally advise the president of the college of the dispatch of K-9 teams(s). A follow- up written report shall be submitted to the appropriate College President, University Deputy Chancellor and the Vice Chancellor for University Relations, furnishing complete information relative to the request, the need for which services, the action taken on the request and the results of the assistance provided.
GUIDELINES ON THE USE OF FORCE IN CANINE DEPLOYMENT
This section is provided to assist K-9 handlers in making appropriate decisions on the deployment of their canine partners when the use of force to effect a lawful arrest becomes necessary.

Courts throughout the United States have consistently and overwhelmingly ruled that when a properly trained police canine is used to apprehend a suspect and effectuate his/her lawful arrest, that the canine’s actions are considered minimal force.

It is imperative that handlers fully understand that they may only use that amount of force which is necessary to effect a lawful arrest. Therefore, the deployment of police canines to effect lawful arrests should only be considered when the use of force would be justified in effecting the arrest.

In most situations where the handler has commanded his/her canine partner to make a physical apprehension, the handler has the ability to recall his/her canine if such circumstances arise, thereby terminating the apprehension command. Unlike the discharge of a firearm which can never be recalled once fired, this unique ability affords the protection to all person(s) involved in the potentially dangerous process of effecting a lawful arrest.

K-9 Teams shall not be used to search abandoned or closed buildings or premises solely for trespassers or others suspected of committing disorderly persons offenses or violations as defined in the New York State Penal Law.

Probable cause and Justifiable Use of Force Public Safety canines trained to effect physical apprehensions may be used to apprehend escaped criminals, as well as to apprehend criminals where the officer/handler has probable cause to arrest the subject and where the use of force is justified.

The fact that a suspect is fleeing and/or hiding themselves creates a potentially dangerous situation for pursuing peace officers. Peace officers are at a strategic disadvantage when pursuing a fleeing suspect or attempting to locate one that is hiding since;
I) It is usually unknown if the suspect is or has become armed, and/or;
II) If the suspect plans to inflict harm on or upon the pursuing peace officers and/or the public.
Restrictions on Off Lead Apprehensions The chase apprehension may be conducted with the canine off lead only under the following circumstances:
There are no other persons who will be endangered by the release of the canine; and;

An appropriate warning is given prior to release of the canine identifying the presence of the peace officer, which warning shall include an announcement that the subject is under arrest and a command that the subject comply with the officer’s directions or else the canine will be released; and
The peace officer handler will insure that the canine has had the opportunity to see the subject intended for arrest; and

The officer handler is able to maintain visual contact with the canine throughout the chase. If during the chase, the officer handler loses visual contact with the canine, or is about to lose visual contact with the canine, the officer handler shall immediately recall the canine.
AUTHORIZED DEPLOYMENT AND USE SITUATIONS FOR POLICE CANINES
When it is believed that unauthorized entry has been gained into a building or a suspect(s) has fled into and concealed themselves in a building, and;
Where probable cause exists to believe that the suspect(s) hiding within have committed a crime as defined by the New York State Penal Law.
The use of force is justified to effectuate the arrest of the suspect(s).

The initial responding officers shall immediately establish a perimeter and exhaust all available efforts to determine if innocent person(s), including public safety personnel, are within the building without entering same.
The initial responding officers shall exhaust all available efforts to avoid further contamination of affected areas unless emergency situations dictate otherwise.
The handler shall make the following search warning announcement upon entering the building and prior to beginning the search with his canine partner (in a loud voice);

“I’M A PEACE OFFICER, YOU’RE UNDER ARREST, I HAVE A TRAINED POLICE DOG. IF YOU DON’T COME OUT, I’ll TURN HIM LOOSE. OFFICERS SHOULD BE COGNIZANT THAT IN SOME AREAS OF COLLEGE BUILDINGS AND PROPERTY, HEARING IMPAIRED INDIVIDUALS MAY BE PRESENT AND THE OFFICER MIGHT NEED TO USE NONVERBAL METHODS TO COMMUNICATE WITH THEM. THESE NONVERBAL METHODS MIGHT INCLUDE: USE OF A FLASHLIGHT, BANGING THE WALL WITH AN ASP TO PRODUCE VIBRATIONS.
The handler will then wait a reasonable period of time, depending on the building size, to allow the suspect (s) to surrender and/or innocent person (s) to exit.
In large offices and/or warehouse type structures, the search warning announcement will be given by the handler prior to commencing the search on each separate floor of the building.
The search will be conducted in a systematic manner as determined by the handler.

All searches will be conducted off lead except when in the opinion of the handler the dog’s safety would be jeopardized; or it is the decision of the handler to employ other officers to assist in the search.

Tracking can be conducted by the K-9 teams for various situations including but not limited to; missing persons, e.g. children, elderly, etc. or suspected criminals who have fled a particular area or location.

The initial responding officers shall immediately establish a perimeter and exhaust all available efforts to determine if innocent and/or unrelated person(s) including other law enforcement personnel are contained within the established perimeter area without entering same.

The initial responding officers shall exhaust available efforts to avoid further contamination of affected areas, especially that in which the individual(s) to be tracked were last seen, unless emergency situations dictate otherwise.

Tracking will be conducted on lead at a sufficient length to be determined by the handler. The handler shall also decide whether or not a back up officer will be utilized on the track based on the particular circumstances of the situations.

Missing children should not be tracked by canines trained to effect physical apprehensions unless the canine handler has a reasonable belief that serious bodily harm or death will occur if the missing child is not located. Where the use of a public safety department canine is deemed necessary and appropriate to track a missing child, the risks to the missing child from the use of the canine shall first be explained by the canine handler to the missing child’s parents, guardian, or next of kin. The approval of a child’s parents, guardian, or next of kin must first be obtained before the canine team is deployed. Prior consent need not be obtained where there is reason to believe that an abduction has occurred or that serious bodily injury or death is imminent without the use of the canine.
When probable cause exists to believe that a suspect(s) has committed a crime as defined by the New York State Penal Law and; the use of force is justified to effectuate the arrest of the suspect(s).
In most situations criminal apprehensions will be accomplished off lead. However, it is important to emphasize that criminal apprehensions can also be accomplished when the canine is still on lead.
Whenever possible, the handler shall allow the suspect(s) to surrender by giving the following warning announcement prior to releasing his/her canine partner (in a loud voice);
“PEACE OFFICER,. YOU’RE UNDER ARREST. STOP OR I WILL RELEASE MY POLICE DOG.”
If the suspect(s) surrenders, the canine apprehension will be terminated, and the suspect(s) will be handcuffed and searched in accordance with existing CUNY public safety training standards.

Under absolutely no circumstance should any public safety personnel other than the handler interfere with the canine once he has been committed to make the apprehension unless specifically directed by the handler.

Once the canine has effected the apprehension, it will hold the suspect until commanded to release by the handler. The canine is trained to maintain a bite during any resistance provided by the suspect.
The handler will immediately advise the suspect to stop fighting and/or resisting the canine, and the handler will command the canine to release the suspect.
Once the suspect has complied and submits to the arrest, the handler will immediately command the canine to release the apprehension and call the canine into a watch position.
The handler will then advise the suspect that if they attempt to assault the peace officers and/or canine, that they will again be apprehended by the canine.

If other officers are available, they will be summoned by the handler to handcuff and search the suspect; otherwise this will be accomplished by the handler who shall leave his canine partner in a watch position. In the event the suspect(s) are handcuffed by the assisting officers, the handler will put the canine on lead before calling in the backup officers.
Once the suspect has been successfully handcuffed and searched, the handler will insure that the suspect(s) are provided with immediate medical attention for any injury sustained during the arrest.
If the suspect refuses medical attention, the suspect(s) will sign the Public Safety Department Medical Treatment Refusal Form.
In the event that the suspect(s) refuses to sign, the handler’s supervisor will be notified, and the supervisor will note that the suspect(s) refusal to sign on the refusal sheet.
This section shall apply to all instances in which the K-9 teams have successfully located and/or apprehended a suspect(s).
When it is believed that an article and/or instrument of a crime has been discarded in a particular area by the suspect(s) involved in the incident, a search should be initiated.

The initial responding officers shall immediately establish a perimeter and exhaust all available efforts to determine if innocent person(s) including police personnel, are contained within the established perimeter area without entering same.
The initial responding officers shall exhaust all available efforts to avoid further contamination of affected areas unless emergency situations dictate otherwise.
The search will be conducted in a systematic manner as determined by the handler.
The handler will decide if the search will be conducted on lead or off lead based on the particular circumstances of the situation.
Under no circumstances shall K-9 team(s) be used for crowd control and/or deterrent effects at the scene of peaceful demonstrations.

The Canine Unit may be deployed to assist the Yonkers Police Department or The New York City Police Department on request and shall be directed by established protocol, through a Memorandum of Understanding. Other agencies making such request will be handled according to Public Safety guidelines relative to K-9 unit utilization.

The Canine Team will demonstrate the ability to conduct proper searches to locate a “suspect,” “subject,” or “evidence” within buildings, interior structures and extended, exterior areas of various terrains.

The canine on command from the canine handler, will both on lead or off lead at the discretion of the handler, search, find, and indicate or retrieve a variety of articles with a human scent (such as clothing, a gun, a wallet, or a screwdriver) within a specified area, including buildings and interior structures and extended, exterior areas of various terrains.

The canine, on command from the canine handler, will both on lead or off lead at the discretion of the handler, search, find and indicate a “suspect” or “subject” within a specified area. Such searches are to include:
The canine handler will recognize the alert signs given by the canine.
The canine, on command from the canine handler, will track (follow) a human scent.
The canine handler will control the canine during searches.

Public demonstrations conducted by the K-9 Unit are usually very well accepted and offer an excellent opportunity for public safety personnel to relate and interact with the University community on a positive note.
Since public acceptance and support of the K-9 Unit is essential to maintaining the professional integrity of the K-9 Unit and the CUNY
Public Safety Department as a whole, all requests for same shall be handled as follows;
Requests shall be directed to the University Director of Public Safety who shall approve and coordinate the request(s) with the K- 9 Unit supervisor.
All reasonable efforts shall be made by K-9 Unit personnel to fulfill all demonstration requests approved by the University Director of Public Safety.
Care shall be taken by all K-9 handler(s) that their appearance and presentation reflect a respectable and professional image on the CUNY Public Safety Department.
K-9 handler(s) shall maintain complete control over their dogs to insure the utmost safety to the public.
Civilian contact with CUNY Public Safety Department dogs should be at the discretion of the handler.

When a suspect or suspects are arrested as a result of a canine search, assisting officers will handle the arrest processing procedure of the suspect(s), so the K-9 team may return to service. If the arrest involves a physical apprehension, the suspect(s) will be processed by the handler who shall in addition to normal processing procedures;
Write a detailed supplementary report explaining the involvement of the K-9 team which shall include, but not be limited to:
The deterrent effect the K-9 team’s presence had on the situation, if any.

Complete documentation and explanation of all situations in which the suspect(s) surrendered as a result of the K-9 teams presence and/or utilization. This report must be submitted to the office of the University Public Safety Director within 24 hours of the incident.

It is imperative that all instances relating to the K-9 teams utilization and/or deterrent effect on any situation be properly and completely documented by the handler on the appropriate report forms.
The completed reports are to be forwarded directly to the Office of the University Public Safety Director within 24 hours. Such situations would include but are not limited to;
DUTIES AND RESPONSIBILITIES OF INITIAL RESPONDING OFFICERS
Upon arrival at all suspected crime scenes or situations, the K-9 officer shall immediately assess the situation to determine if the K-9 Unit could be beneficial to the investigation.

When the initial responding officer(s) and/or supervisor(s) determine that canine assistance is required, they shall take all reasonable actions to insure that appropriate perimeters are established as outlined in this policy and shall gather as much information as possible for the responding K-9 team(s).
Perimeters shall be maintained until relieved by the handler or other competent authority.
Officer (s) maintaining perimeters shall do so as tactically as possible while maintaining the integrity of the secured area and remaining alert to possible hazards.

In all instances where the handler has deployed a canine, whether on-lead or off- lead, all officers must remain completely alert to the canines presence in the area and the potential of the canine to make physical apprehensions.
LIMITATIONS OF CANINES ABILITIES & SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS

Weather conditions such as rain, snow, heat, wind etc. have a tremendous effect on the canines ability to properly function and these factors must be considered when contemplating the use of a K-9 team.

Canines ability to locate human scent is provided through their extraordinary olfactory senses. It is therefore imperative for peace officers at the scene of situations where the use of a K-9 team is being considered to properly protect the scene from further scent contamination.

Canines function to their fullest capabilities when permitted to search off-lead. Canines have an inherent ability to detect scent via the ground/terrain and/or through various air/wind currents that flow through the specific area. The handler must therefore take into account all available information relating to the situation when making their decision to deploy their canine partners on-lead or off-lead in any given situation.
Special consideration for the K-9 team(s) deployment shall be given in all situations involving known barricaded suspect(s) and/or hostage situations.
Applicants for the Public Safety Department Canine Unit must have
At least two years uniform patrol experience with satisfactory work performance, disciplinary and medical leave records;
A willingness to remain with the unit for at least four years;

A willingness (together with other family members) to care for and house the canine at the officer’s residence with a secure outdoor area for the canine that conforms with CUNY Public Safety requirements;
A strong desire to work with canines and willingness to care for and train the animal; and
The ability to pass designated physical fitness and agility exams related to the task of canine handling.

The Deputy University Public Safety Director and the canine supervisory lieutenant shall be responsible for selection of canine handlers in accordance with established public safety department procedures.
All public safety department canines must meet established New York State Bureau of Municipal Police established certification requirements. Untrained canines may not be used for canine duty.
New canine handlers must complete the prescribed 17 week New York State Bureau of Municipal Police Canine Handlers course and successfully meet all course requirements.
Canine handlers are required to demonstrate acquired abilities to the canine supervisor on a periodic basis as prescribed in this public safety service operation instruction.

All canines on patrol and canines trained to effect physical apprehensions shall be maintained by only one handler. If the canine’s handler is sick or unavailable for duty, that canine shall not be used by another handler or the service for any purpose.
Overall supervision of the K-9 Unit will be the responsibility of the K-9 Unit University Central Office Supervisory Lieutenant through the appropriate chain- of-command.

Immediate supervision of K-9 Unit personnel assigned to deterrent and/or related patrol duties will be the responsibility of the on-duty College Public Safety Tour Commander(s) or College Public Safety Director.
K-9 Unit response to assist other agencies will be supervised by the University Director of Public Safety and/or his designee.
GENERAL OPERATIONAL ORDERS FOR CANINE PERSONNEL

Personnel assigned to the K-9 Unit, in addition to complying with University public safety instructions and other college public safety orders, have the added responsibility of handling and caring for a trained police dog.

A trained police dog used carelessly or improperly is a dangerous weapon and could subject both the handler and the University to both criminal and civil court actions, as well as reflecting discredit upon the entire CUNY Public Safety Department.

With anticipation of keeping injuries to both sworn public safety personnel and civilians at an absolute minimum, while further developing the K-9 Unit into an efficient and well organized elite Unit of the University Public Safety Department the following orders are issued to all personnel of the K-9 Unit;
All personnel of the K-9 Unit shall wear the proper K-9 Unit uniform of the day with their badge and name plate displayed at all times during their tour of duty.

All dogs, when unattended in the Yonkers Police Department Training Center, shall either be placed back into their run or tied to allotted spaces within the unit pad. Care shall be taken to assure that the dogs cannot injure persons, each other, or themselves.
All dogs, when unattended shall be placed in the college canine holding kennel. Care shall be taken to assure that the dogs cannot injure persons, each other, or themselves.
All dogs are to be kept as quiet as possible both on-duty and off-duty.

All dogs assigned to handlers who house their dogs at home shall be aware of criminal and civil actions which could result from carelessness in the event their dogs bite an innocent persons(s) off-duty. Handlers shall also take extra precautions to insure that their dog is not allowed to roam the streets unattended or off lead to prevent accidental injury by a passing automobile.
During training, no one will be allowed to leave the training area while on- duty without obtaining permission from competent training authority.

The college kennels are off-limits to all except authorized handlers, K-9 officials, trainers, or supervisory personnel of the K-9 Unit. No handler is permitted to bring visitor(s) to the kennel without specific permission from the University Director of Public Safety.
All handlers are to groom their dogs daily, including complete physical examinations for injuries and/or infestations such as; fleas, ticks, etc.
All handlers are to insure that the general health and hygiene and care of their assigned canine(s) is properly maintained and that periodic veterinary examinations are provided.
All dogs shall be exercised in an area provided for them where they can empty at will.

Abuse of dogs in any way is a violation of New York State Law and will not be tolerated. All injuries or sickness of assigned canines are to be promptly reported to the canine supervisory sergeant, who shall insure that the proper and immediate care is given and the appropriate reports are submitted.
Handlers are reminded that the dogs of the K-9 Unit are the property of The City University of New York and shall not be used for stud services.
No dog shall be used in any freshly painted building where paint fumes still linger.
No dog shall be entered in any show, trial or exhibition without express permission from the University Director of Public Safety or his representative.
Careless handling of dogs at any time is strictly prohibited.
The feeding of dogs by the public is to be politely discouraged.

Unless necessary in the performance of duty, agitation or criminal apprehension will only be done under the supervision of a certified CUNY public safety trainer. The teasing of a dog at any time will not be tolerated.

All dog apprehensions, regardless of where they occurred, or how minor they appear, shall be reported to the University Director of Public Safety immediately. Upon notification, the supervisory officer shall be responsible for submitting all required reports and recommendations to the University Director of Public Safety within 24 hours of the incident.

Discretion is to be used by all handlers to prevent dogs from defecating in or near public and/or private buildings either on duty or off duty. Removal of canine solid waste is required pursuant to city health code and on all CUNY property.
Dogs will not be allowed to drink from any public drinking fountain pools, or stagnant puddles, nor shall they be permitted to wade or swim in any pool unless in the performance of their duties.

Periodic visits shall be made to the homes of handlers who keep their dogs at home by the Deputy University Director of Public Safety, or his designee, or K-9 supervisory Lieutenant, for reasons of health, sanitation, and security.
Members of the K-9 Unit shall perform such other duties as they may be called upon to perform by competent authority.
Handlers will keep the K-9 vans passenger and rear doors locked at all times. The driver’s door will be locked when the handler is out of the vehicle.
Windows on the K-9 vans passenger and driver’s side shall be cracked no more than three inches in order to prevent the canines head to protrude outside of the patrol vehicle while parked and locked.

It shall be the responsibility of each handler to immediately notify the K-9 Unit supervisor(s) of any type of problems and/or difficulties he/she has experienced with their canines for appropriate action.
It shall also be the responsibility of each handler to attend the required amount of annual in-service training as well as any other training required by competent authority.

Member of the canine unit who are away on vacation or out of town for other reasons, must get permission from the Office of the University Director of Public Safety to take the canine along. Otherwise the canine will be housed at an authorized kennel until the handler returns. No family member, relative or friend will be allowed to provide extended care for any CUNY canine.
AREAS OF ASSIGNMENT AND PROCEDURES FOR REPORTING ON/OFF- DUTY

Handling specific K-9 Unit assignments, K-9 teams are to be assigned during the 11:00 PM to 7:00 AM tour unless otherwise authorized or requested by a college president or when handling specific K-9 Unit training assignments, University/College sponsored programs or deployed to assist outside law enforcement agencies. K-9 units may respond as back-up units on the following calls:
Crimes in progress; i.e. purse snatching burglaries, robberies, etc.
The canine unit may be used to provide escort to and from subways or remote areas on campus and parking lots. A Canine Unit handler is not to be used to escort money drops.
K-9 teams will not be used for service type calls that will take them out of service for extended periods of time.
K-9 officers are not to be used for meal reliefs.
“OFFICER DOWN” ASSISTANCE FOR HANDLER AND/OR CANINE
In the event that a K-9 officer or canine is severely injured to the point where assistance is required, the following procedure will be followed;
The canine handler, if able, will contact the college communications desk stating the problem, and will request assistance.

In the event that the handler is not able to request assistance, then the first arriving officer will advise the supervisor and immediately inform the college communications desk that the canine handler requires assistance.

The communications desk will immediately notify the duty tour commander and K-9 supervisory sergeant, as to the nature of the assistance required, and the location of the assistance. The lieutenant will be required to either be at a telephone number, or be available on pager if not on duty.
It will be the responsibility of the K-9 supervisory sergeant to immediately respond to the scene and either remove the dog from the vehicle, affected area, or assist the handler.
In the event that the situation arises where there is no time for K-9 supervisory sergeant or the trainer to respond, then another working canine officer will be authorized to assist.

The K-9 supervisory sergeant, or other canine officer will remove the canine from the premises and place the dog in the kennels as soon as it is practical. The dog will remain in the college public safety kennels until the handler returns to pick up the canine, or a decision is made by a certified canine trainer.
All members of the CUNY Public Safety Department shall adhere to this directive and all supervisors of the Department shall be responsible and accountable for said adherence.

inst.title: Bomb Threats Response Procedure
b: Bombs, explosive devices and bomb threats pose serious public safety problems to colleges and other public and high profile institutions. Extremists have bombed many facilities since 1980 and an even greater number of bomb threats, a form of harassment, have been received. This instruction will outline public safety steps to ease the panic and disorder that a bomb threat can cause.

A BOMB IS AN EXPLOSIVE DEVICE FUSED TO DETONATE UNDER SPECIFIED CONDITIONS. The most common explosive materials are dynamite, TNT, nitroglycerin, gun/blasting powder and plastique. Since they are so compact, today's bomb can easily be hidden. A quart size explosive can do considerable damage, to say nothing of the chain reaction it may trigger. Pipe bombs and plastic charges are even smaller. Placement for maximum damage depends on the skill, daring, and fanaticism of the bomber. Stairways, rest rooms and storerooms are likely hiding places if they are accessible to the public.

Delivery of a bomb to a specific site is the chief concern of public safety personnel. Once placed, the bomb is a real menace. The more vulnerable a facility is, the more it should be shielded from incursion. To complicate matters, sometimes an explosive device may be delivered by mail. (see the last page for mail bomb precautions).

Most bomb threats are delivered by telephone. The would-be bomber usually calls when someone can react to the threat. The phone offers the caller a cloak of secrecy. Each threat must be handled as if it is genuine, although most often it is a hoax. The public safety officer who receives a call that a bomb has been planted at the facility where he/she is assigned should:
Fill in the "Bomb Threat Checklist" (copy attached) while the caller is on the telephone or as soon as practical while the details are still fresh.
Try to induce conversation. Keep the caller on the line as long as possible. Don't interrupt, except to ask the caller to speak louder, slower or to repeat.

Ask as many questions as possible utilizing the "Bomb Threat Checklist", and the list of additional questions (see last two pages of this instruction). Show levelheaded concern. Information on when and where the bomb is set to explode is of paramount importance. If the caller reveals this vital information, try to alert public safety management while the threat is still in progress. If a fellow officer is nearby, use a code word or hand gesture to get their attention.
Listen closely to the caller's message, voice and background noises. Take notes. Try to record the caller's exact words. Keep the callers talking as long as possible.
Start the notification chain. Immediately notify the Tour Commander and Public Safety Administrator. One of them may authorize calling the police.
Never abandon a post in search of a bomb. Await directions.

To locate a bomb, a good plan includes a search procedure. With all possible haste, appropriate law enforcement officials should be called to the scene to direct the search for a bomb. The New York City Police Department has officers specially trained and experienced in bomb threat investigations.

If the location of a threatened bomb is unknown and urgency dictates a search of critical areas until proper authorities arrive, this should be done by trained search teams and the search should be conducted in a painstaking manner. When the threat indicates that the bomb has been placed in a specific area, the search should start there.

When a two-person search team enters the room to be searched, they should first move to various parts of the room and stand quietly with their eyes closed and listen for a clockwork device. Frequently, a clockwork mechanism can be quickly detected without the use of special equipment. Even if no clockwork mechanism is detected, the team is now aware of the background noise level within the room itself.

The officer in charge of the search team should attempt to enlist the aid of the room/area occupants who are familiar with unusual packages in their area. The officer will then look around the room and determine how the room is to be divided for searching and to what height the first search sweep should extend. The first search sweep will cover all items resting on the floor up to the selected height. The second sweep will include the remaining areas. The room should be divided into two parts with an officer assigned to search each area.
Divide the area and select a search height.
Start from the bottom and work up.
Start back to back and work toward each other.
Go around the walls and proceed toward the center of the room.

No piece of furniture or equipment should be taken for granted. Sound or speaker systems, fixtures, bookcases, air conditioners, exposed beams, etc., should be inspected. Do not rely exclusively on random or spot checking of logical target areas. The bomber may not be a logical person.

Have a sign or marker indicating “search completed” conspicuously posted in the area. Place a piece of colored tape across the door approximately two feet above the floor if the use of signs is not practical.
ACTIONS TO BE TAKEN IF A SUSPECTED OBJECT IS FOUND

DO NOT MOVE, JAR, TOUCH, TAMPER OR INTERFERE WITH THE OBJECT IN ANY WAY OR ANYTHING ATTACHED TO IT; THE REMOVING AND DISARMING OF A BOMB MUST BE LEFT TO PROFESSIONALS WHO SPECIALIZE IN EXPLOSIVES DETECTION, DISARMING AND REMOVAL, I.E. NYPD BOMB SQUAD.
NOTIFY THE NEW YORK CITY POLICE DEPARTMENT IMMEDIATELY.
EVACUATE THE BUILDING TACTFULLY; EVERY EFFORT SHOULD BE MADE TO AVOID PANIC.
PENDING THE ARRIVAL OF THE POLICE, ENDEAVOR TO PREVENT PERSONS FROM ENTERING THE THREATENED PREMISE.
DO NOT TRANSMIT MESSAGES VIA WALKIE TALKIE IN THE AREA WHERE THE SUSPECTED OBJECT IS FOUND; USE TELEPHONE LINES TO COMMUNICATE.
