inst.title: eJusticeNY Integrated Justice Portal
b: The eJusticeNY Integrated Justice Portal is a secure extranet that provides authorized users with quick and easy access to all available public safety and criminal justice information when and where it is needed. The Portal provides a single interface through which users can access information from a variety of federal, state and local sources; in addition also providing access to civil data.
To establish guidelines for the security and integrity of the eJusticeNY Integrated Justice Portal and the dissemination derived from it.

Portal: The eJusticeNY Integrated Justice Portal is the computerized system administered by a joint team led by the New York State Police. The system includes the equipment, facilities, procedures, agreements, and organizations thereof for the collection, processing, preservation, or dissemination of criminal justice information.

Criminal Justice Purpose: When obtaining CHRI, criminal justice purpose means accessing information available through the Portal as part of an official duty associated with the administration of criminal justice (Title 28 CFR 20.3 (d)). When accessing information available through the Portal for an official function, including training, normally performed by criminal justice employees.
ORI: An Originating Agency Identifier (ORI) is a nine (9) character alphanumeric code assigned to criminal justice, law enforcement, and non-criminal justice agencies by NCIC.
TAC: Terminal Agency Coordinator (TAC), responsible for organizing, coordinating, and overseeing all Portal related logistics necessary to maintain and support Portal end-users within their agency.
HIT: A hit is a positive response from NCIC in which the person or property inquired upon appears to match the person or property contained in the response.

A College Public Safety Director must make a written request to the TAC for user credentials on behalf of a member of service to gain access to the Portal. Upon receiving Portal access, all members of service must pass the Use & Dissemination Examination; this examination is made available through the Portal.

Regardless of the user’s level, re-certification is required every two (2) years from the date of examination. It is the responsibility of the TAC to ensure that all users are notified prior to their expiration to re-certify. Study materials are available for preparation of the Use & Dissemination examination.

The Portal Terminal Agency Coordinator (TAC) is responsible for organizing, coordinating, and overseeing all Portal related logistics necessary to maintain and support Portal end-users within our department.

The TAC is the primary point of contact at the agency level; and has the vital role of directly assigning the appropriate access to each user. The TAC is also the point of contact for all central administration requests regarding system access and all related correspondence. The TAC can be contacted via the University of Office of Public Safety.
All operators must abide by Portal security rules in conjunction with the Portal Code of Ethics; which is available in the Use & Dissemination Rules & Regulations Student Guide. All operators:
Shall ensure that no information received through the Portal is disseminated to anyone outside the Criminal Justice System unless directed by an appropriate court or other legal authority;

Shall ensure that all printed matter received over the Portal is properly destroyed; by means of shredding or in another manner that renders the material unreadable, once the information is no longer current or pertinent to the Departments interest;
Shall transmit only authorized messages via the Portal that are to be used for Criminal Justices purposes;
Shall ensure that inquiries made via the Portal are for Criminal Justice purposes ONLY;

Shall verbally report any actual, suspected, or attempted Portal security breaches to a supervisor and the TAC immediately, in addition, the Member of Service must submit a written notification, in the form of an incident report of such act within 24 hours. When a reported attempt to breach security of the Portal is received, the TAC shall; notify the University Director of Public Safety or designee, and under their direction contact Department of Criminal Justice Services (DCJS) providing as much of the following information as possible;
Type of information requested (i.e. DMV, CCH, address, etc.)
Specific information requested (i.e. Name, Registration number, etc.)
Name and title of person attempting to access
Agency name used by person attempting access
Call back number and ORI used by the person attempting the access
Was an attempt to make a call back to number given made?

A Portal positive response or "hit" alone is not probable or reasonable cause to arrest. While the information contained in a hit may be presumed to be accurate, it still must be evaluated to determine what, if any, action is appropriate. Operators who receive a hit confirmation must:
Ensure that the person or property inquired upon is identical to the person or property identified in the record;
Contact the originating agency of the record and confirm if the hit is still active. It is the operator’s responsibility to contact the requesting agency within the specific time frames below.

Routine Request: This request must be confirmed within one hour, routine response is to be used when the arresting/locating agency has charges of their own on the subject and the subject is going to be detained by them in addition to warrant entry.

Urgent Request: This request must be confirmed within 10 minutes. An urgent response is to be used when the arresting/locating agency does not have their own charges on the subject and they are not detaining the person for any other reason than the warrant entry.

inst.title: Naloxone Hydrochloride Deployment
b: The purpose of this policy is to set out the requirements for the administration of naloxone by trained members of the service. The objective is to treat and reduce injuries and fatalities due to opioid–involved overdoses when members of the service first arrive at the scene of a suspected overdose.

It is the policy of the Department of Public Safety that members of the service who administer naloxone must complete an initial training by an authorized Opioid Overdose Prevention Program and, every two years thereafter, complete a refresher training program, in accordance with New York State Public Health Law §3309 and the Rules and Regulations on Controlled Substances, Title 10, §80.138 Codes, Rules and Regulations of the State of New York.
The Department of Public Safety Training Academy will provide members with training that meets the standards set forth in the law and regulations.

Opioid: A medication or drug that is derived from the opium poppy or that mimics the effect of an opiate. Opiate drugs are narcotic sedatives that depress activity of the central nervous system; these will reduce pain, induce sleep, and in overdose, will cause people to stop breathing. First responders often encounter opiates in the form of morphine, methadone, codeine, heroin, fentanyl, oxycodone (OxyContin®, Percocet®, and Percocet®), and hydrocodone (Vicodin®).

Naloxone: A prescription medication that can be used to reverse the effects of an opiate overdose. Specifically, it displaces opioids from the receptors in the brain that control the central nervous system and respiratory system. It is marketed under various trademarks, including Narcan®.
Overdose Rescue Kit: At minimum, should include the following:
Two (2) prefilled luer-lock syringes, without needles, each containing 2mg of naloxone in 2ml of solution, and within their manufacturer assigned expiration dates.
Two (2) mucosal atomizer device (MAD) tips, compatible with standard luer-lock syringes.
The Department of Public Safety Training Academy will ensure that the members of the service carrying or having access to the Overdose Rescue Kits are trained in the use of the naloxone.

The Department of Public Safety Training Academy also will ensure that each member of the service carrying or having access to the Overdose Rescue Kits receive refresher training at least every two years that is consistent with the opioid overdose prevention training curriculum.

The Department of Public Safety Training Academy will be responsible for maintaining records relating to training, including the names of the trained overdose responders and the dates they were trained. In addition, The Department of Public Safety Training Academy will notify members and the Director of Public Safety at the campus where each member is employed about the need for refresher training.

It is the responsibility of the Director of Public Safety at each campus to ensure that members do not carry or have access to the Overdose Rescue Kits unless they complete the initial training and later complete refresher training.

The Director of Public Safety at each campus will provide the University Director of Public Safety with the identity of the individual who will serve as the coordinator for the naloxone administration program.
Assuring the supply, integrity and expiration dates of the Overdose Rescue Kits and;
Assuring the maintenance of the administration records.
Request an ambulance to respond to the scene where the aided is in a potential overdose state and inform EMS personnel upon their arrival if naloxone has been administered.
Use universal precautions and protections from blood borne pathogens and communicable diseases when administering naloxone.

Determine need for treatment with naloxone by evaluating the aided: if the aided is unresponsive with decreased or absent respirations they should administer naloxone following the established training guidelines.

Complete an assessment of the aided; which should include, but may not be limited to determining unresponsiveness and other indicators of opioid involved overdose, the officer will administer the medication from the Overdose Rescue Kit following the established training guidelines.

Use proper tactics when administering naloxone; aided individuals who are revived from an opioid overdose may regain consciousness in an agitated and combative state and may exhibit symptoms associated with withdrawal.
Remain with the aided until EMS personnel arrive.
Each Member of the Service will be responsible for inspecting the kit assigned to him/her, for signs of damage and to ensure the kit has not expired.
If a kit is lost, damaged or expired, the member shall report this to the campus coordinator of the naloxone administration program for a replacement.
Damaged or expired naloxone must be returned to the Office of the University Director of Public Safety from the campus coordinator for proper disposal.

Overdose Rescue Kits will be carried in a manner consistent with proper storage guidelines for temperature and sunlight exposure. Extreme temperatures, both high and low may be damaging to naloxone. Due to this fact, consideration should be given when storing in the interior of a patrol car.
A Member of the service must report all responses to victims of suspected drug overdose to the opioid overdose prevention program Director or designee.

Subsequent to administering naloxone, a Member of the service is required to complete the following forms: a. New York State Public Safety Naloxone Quality Improvement Usage Report b. University Incident Report
The Naloxone Administration/Restock form will be submitted by the University Director of Public Safety (or designee) to the New York State Department of Health as needed.

inst.title: Violent Felony and Sexual Assault Investigations
b: The purpose of this section of the CUNY Public Safety Operations Guide is ensure compliance with CUNY’s Plan and Procedures for the Investigation and Reporting of Violent Felonies which establishes procedures that the Department of Public Safety will follow when informed of a violent felony offense on campus.

NYPD will be notified immediately via 911 and/or via NYPD portable radio. The appropriate number of officers/supervisors will be dispatched to the scene immediately in an effort to stop the offense, protect and aid the victim and if possible, apprehend the perpetrator of the offense.
CUNY Public Safety Officers will cooperate with the NYPD or other law enforcement officers to:
Protect and aid the alleged victim(s)
Attempt to apprehend the alleged perpetrator(s)
Direct students, staff or other visitors to a safe location
Assist individuals who need medical treatment by arranging for transportation to the hospital by EMS; and
If necessary, and to the extent possible, obtain medical treatment for those in need on the scene, until EMS arrives.
If there is an on-going threat of danger to the college community or any other CUNY campus, a CUNY Alert will be generated.
In addition, whenever there is a threat to another CUNY campus, the Director of Public Safety at the threatened campuses will be notified directly.

If a CUNY campus and/or University Public Safety Department receives a report of a violent felony that occurred on a CUNY campus in the past and no immediate danger is posed to the CUNY community, the Public Safety Department will respond and gather all available information. Public Safety will report the past violent felony offense to the New York City Police Department (NYPD) as soon as practicable but in no case more than twenty-four hours after receiving the report, except in cases where federal or state law, including, but not limited to, the federal Campus Sexual Assault Victims’ Bill of Rights under Title 20 U.S. Code Section 1092(f), gives the victim of a sexual offense the right to determine whether or not to report the incident to law enforcement.

The CUNY Public Safety Operations Guide, section 13, will guide the process regarding notification of CUNY personnel. In addition to following the above referenced section of the Public Safety Operations Guide, as set forth above, the NYPD will be notified whenever a report that a violent felony has occurred on campus is received, no later than 24 hours after that report is received, except in cases where federal or state law, including but not limited to, the Federal Campus Sexual Assault Victims’ Bill of Rights, contained in 20 U.S.C. section 1092 (f), gives the complainant the right to determine whether to report the incident to law enforcement. In addition, the following must be notified of the report:
Vice President for Finance and Administration
Any others as deemed appropriate as dictated by the circumstances
Campus Title IX Coordinator, if the incident involves sexual or domestic violence or stalking of a sexual nature.
When appropriate, an emergency notification or timely warning will be issued to the appropriate campus or campuses.

The scene of the offense will be secured as quickly as possible for possible forensic examination by NYPD. The area will be restricted to only those who must enter. The names and contact information of those entering the crime scene will be recorded.

If it becomes known that a CUNY computer or other electronic device and/or CUNY electronic account was used to perpetrate the offense, the appropriate individuals will be contacted in an effort to secure and preserve the computer, device and/or electronic account.
If CUNY surveillance video of the scene of the offense is available, it will be preserved.
Responding officers will conduct interviews to determine if a violent felony has taken place and if so to identify the perpetrator. The names and contact information of witnesses will be recorded.

If the victim’s identity is known or discovered, campus public safety officials will provide appropriate support and assistance to the victim, including, where appropriate, assistance in obtaining medical attention, preserving evidence, reporting to the NYPD or other law enforcement agents, and other security measures. Where appropriate, in cases involving violent felonies of a sexual nature, public safety officials will also offer to provide the victim with transportation to a SAFE hospital.

All complainants/victims, including, but not limited to those reporting a sex crime, will be treated with sensitivity. Complainants/victims reporting a sex crime will be provided with information regarding on and off-campus resources.
All complainants/victims will be reminded of the importance of evidence preservation. In particular, complainants/victims reporting sex crimes will be

encouraged to preserve any possible evidence, including clothing, electronic communications, voice mails, text messages or other electronic communications. Where appropriate, they will also be advised as follows:
Do not shower or wash or brush teeth
If the attack took place in a dorm room or other indoor area, do not rearrange any furniture or objects.
Seek medical attention immediately so evidence is preserved. Ask for a rape exam if warranted under the circumstances.

Public Safety will strongly encourage, but will not require the complainant/victim of a sex crime to report the attack to NYPD. While encouraging the complainant/victim to report to the NYPD, Public Safety will also advise the complainant/victim that the choice is his/hers to make. Public Safety will assist promptly complainants/victims who wish to report to the NYPD. Complainants/victims who decide not to make a police report will be informed that their case can be reported at a later time and will be given appropriate information about the timing and process for doing so.
The Director of Public Safety or his/her designee will act as a liaison with the NYPD or other law enforcement agencies and assist with the investigation as necessary.

In cases that are investigated by the NYPD or other law enforcement agencies, all evidence and information collected by the campus Public Safety Department will be provided to the investigating agency.

The Campus will cooperate with all requests for information from the NYPD or other law enforcement agencies. The Campus will attempt to comply with any request by the NYPD and/or other law enforcement agents to delay for a reasonable period of time its own investigation pending the law enforcement investigation. However, in certain circumstances, the Campus may be required to continue its investigation in order to take appropriate remedial measures and/or provide appropriate assistance to the victim. In such cases, the Campus will inform the NYPD and/or other law enforcements about the continued investigation and, if requested and to the extent permissible by law, will share the information
obtained during the Campus investigation with the NYPD and/or other law enforcement agents.

A report containing all pertinent information materials will be filed in the Public Safety incident reporting system. Hard copies of the investigation will be kept on file at the college of occurrence.

inst.title: Missing Person Investigations
b: The purpose of this section of the CUNY Public Safety Operations Guide on Missing Persons is to ensure compliance with CUNY’s Plan and Procedures for the Investigation and Reporting of Missing Persons. The Plan and Procedures for the Investigation and Reporting of Missing Persons establishes official notification procedures for missing students who reside in on-campus housing and ensures that a student who resides in on- campus housing is informed of his/her options under section 485(j) of the Higher Education Act.
Missing Person A student is deemed a “missing person” when the student is a current on-campus housing resident and he or she has been unreachable for more than 24 hours without any known reason.
On-Campus Housing Residence halls operated by CUNY or operated by a private management company on behalf of CUNY.

Each CUNY student who resides in on-campus housing must identify a contact individual (“emergency contact”) who will be contacted no later than 24 hours from the time the student is determined missing. A student may designate his or her emergency contact on the application for residence in on-campus housing. The student’s designated emergency contact information will be kept confidential and will be retained by the campus Residence Life Office and the Department of Public Safety. The emergency contact information will be used only when the student is determined to be a missing person or in other emergency situations.

Students who are under the age of 18 and who are not emancipated must designate an emergency contact. However, in the event that such a student is determined to be a missing person, the campus must, in addition to providing notice to the emergency contact, also notify the student’s custodial parent or legal guardian, if the parent or guardian is not listed as the emergency contact, no later than 24 hours after the student is determined missing.
A student’s designation of an emergency contact will remain in effect until changed or revoked by the student.
The CUNY Public Safety Operations Guide, section 13, will guide the notification process.

In addition, upon receiving information that a student who is an on-campus housing resident may be missing, the Department of Public Safety must contact appropriate campus staff (e.g. the Campus Director of Residence Life) to aid in the search for the student.
As soon as feasible, the following college administrators also will be notified:
Vice President for Finance and Administration
Any others as deemed appropriate as dictated by the circumstances

If, after investigation, the campus Department of Public Safety determines that the student is missing, it must, after consultation with the campus Office of Student Services/Affairs, designate a campus official to contact the missing student’s emergency contact. This contact must be initiated no later than 24 hours after the time the student is determined missing.
Missing Persons Under the Age of 18

If the student who is determined to be a missing person is under 18 and not emancipated, the designated campus official must, in addition to contacting the emergency contact, immediately contact the missing student’s parent or legal guardian, if the parent or guardian is not listed as the emergency contact.
Missing Persons Without a Reachable Designated Emergency Contact
If the missing student’s emergency contact is not reasonably reachable, the designated campus official must inform the New York City Police Department
that the student is missing. Such notification must be done no later than 24 hours after the time the student is determined to be missing.

inst.title: Locker Use By CUNY Employees
b: The purpose of this section is to establish policies of the use of lockers owned by CUNY for its employees and procedures of locker inspections and searches.

CUNY provides lockers to some employees within designated departments as a convenience for temporary storage of personal belongings during the workday. Managers or supervisors in departments with locker space available to employees will assign lockers to eligible employees and maintain a written record of the assigned locker numbers. Lockers are the property of CUNY. Employees who are assigned CUNY lockers do not own or have a property interest in the assigned lockers. Employees are responsible for all items placed in a locker and CUNY will not be responsible for any loss or damage to items stored in the locker. Employees must empty contents of the assigned locker as instructed by managers or supervisors for the purposes of cleaning and general maintenance. Employees are also required to empty lockers upon termination of employment.

Assigned lockers are subject to inspection by managers or supervisors at any time and without advanced notice to employees. Such inspections will take place in the presence of the employees to whom the lockers are assigned. Employees are required to make their lockers available for inspection when they are notified of an inspection. CUNY may forcibly open the locker of any employee who fails to comply with this requirement, and in such instances, may do so outside the presence of the employee.

Lockers also may be opened at the discretion of the College’s or CUNY’s Public Safety Director and/or his/her designee under the following conditions. Lockers will be forcibly opened by CUNY Public Safety personnel if CUNY personnel suspect that the contents of the locker, may produce evidence of a violation of state or federal law, CUNY policy or employee misconduct or contain material that poses a safety risk. In such instances the lockers may be opened outside the presence of the employee, and, to the extent personal items such as wallets, bags or pocket books are stored in the locker, these items may be opened if CUNY personnel suspect that they contain evidence of a violation of state or federal law, CUNY policy or employee misconduct or contain material that poses a safety risk.

inst.title: Post-Use of An Automatic External Defibrillator
b: The purpose of this policy is to assist in understanding the notification process that is required after use of any automatic external defibrillator (AED) owned by The City University of New York.

It is the policy of the Department of Public Safety that, after use of any university owned AED by a member of the college community, including by members of the service, the University’s Medical Director must be notified and provided with a report of the incident, in accordance with the provisions of Chapter 552 of the Laws of 1998 (New York State Public Health Law, Article 30, Section 3000-b) authorizing Public Access Defibrillation and Operations Instruction #13, Public Safety Notifications.

AED: An automatic external defibrillator capable of cardiac rhythm analysis, which will charge and deliver a shock after electronically detecting and assessing ventricular fibrillation or rapid ventricular tachycardia when applied to an unresponsive patient with absent respirations or only gasping and no signs of circulation.

Medical Director: Prescribing physician who is licensed and has issued a written order for the use of AED’s at the City University of New York and ensures that all AED regulatory requirements are implemented.
The City University of New York’s Medical Director requires that post-use of any university owned AED, the following must be completed.

Notification The University’s Medical Director must be contacted on his cellphone. He can be reached at: Medical Director Mark E. Horowitz, MD 200 West 57th Street, Suite 1202 New York, New York 10019 Office Phone: (212) 262-9285 Cellphone: (917) 355-3620

Reporting The electronic data regarding the event that is stored in the AED after its use must be downloaded and forwarded to the Medical Director. The Medical Director also must be provided with a completed copy of the Quality Assurance Report Post- Use of an Automated External Defibrillator form (Appendix A). The downloaded data and Quality Assurance Report must be provided to the Medical Director within 48 hours of the time of the event.
If assistance is required in downloading the data from the AED contact the University Office of Public Safety.

The Medical Director will provide a signed copy of the Quality Assurance Report Post-Use of an Automated External Defibrillator form to the University Office of Public Safety which must then be submitted to The Regional Emergency Medical Services Council of New York City.

inst.title: Procedures for Title IX Related Incidents
b: Every member of The City University of New York community, including students, employees and visitors, deserves the opportunity to live, learn and work free from sex discrimination, sexual harassment, gender-based harassment and sexual violence.

It is the policy of the University—applicable to all colleges and units— to recruit, employ, retain, promote, and provide benefits to employees (including paid and unpaid interns) and to admit and provide services for students without discriminating on the basis of sex. Sex is broadly defined to include sexual orientation, gender and gender identity (including transgender status) as well as pregnancy, childbirth and related medical conditions. Sexual harassment, gender-based harassment and sexual violence, collectively referred to as “sexual misconduct”, are forms of sex discrimination specifically prohibited by this policy.
Defining conduct that constitutes prohibited sex discrimination and sexual misconduct;
Providing clear guidelines for students, employees and visitors on how to report incidents of sex discrimination and sexual misconduct;

Promptly responding to and investigating allegations of sex discrimination and sexual misconduct, pursuing disciplinary action when appropriate, referring the incident to local law enforcement when appropriate, and taking action to investigate and address any allegations of retaliation;
Providing ongoing assistance and support to students and employees who make allegations of sex discrimination and sexual misconduct;

Providing awareness and prevention information on sex discrimination and sexual misconduct, including widely disseminating this policy, as well as a “students’ bill of rights” and implementing training and educational programs on sex discrimination and sexual misconduct; and
Gathering and analyzing information and data that will be reviewed in order to improve safety, reporting, responsiveness and the resolution of incidents.

The Policy on Sexual Misconduct is the sole policy at CUNY addressing sex discrimination and sexual misconduct, and is applicable at all college and units at the University. It will be interpreted in accordance with the principles of academic freedom

adopted by CUNY’s Board of Trustees. In accordance with federal, state and local law, discrimination based on numerous other protected characteristics is prohibited under CUNY’s Policy on Equal Opportunity and Nondiscrimination.

The purpose of this section of the Operations Guide is to highlight the CUNY Policy on Sexual Misconduct and reiterate that all Members of the Service will follow the Policy when responding to incidents of sexual misconduct.

Title IX: The Education Amendments of 1972 which protects people from discrimination based on sex in education programs or activities that receive Federal financial assistance. Title IX states that no person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.

SAFE Hospital: The Sexual Assault Forensic Examiner (SAFE) program philosophy is based upon the belief that providing a specialized standard of medical care and evidence collection to victims of sexual assault will support recovery and prevent further injury or illness arising from victimization, and may increase the successful prosecution of sex offenders for victims who choose to report crimes to law enforcement.
When receiving and responding to a complaint of sexual harassment, gender-based harassment, or sexual violence Members of the Service must:
Determine all the details surrounding not only the incident itself, but also the details regarding what happened before and after the incident.
Determine the relationship of complainant and respondent.
Preserve any possible evidence, including clothing, electronic communications, voicemails (when preserving clothing store in paper bag if possible).
Advise the complainant not to shower or wash and not to brush his/her teeth.
Inform the complainant not to rearrange any furniture or objects if the attack took place in a dorm room or other indoor area.
Recommend that the complaint seek medical attention at a SAFE hospital immediately in order to preserve evidence and when possible request a rape exam.
Assist with option of filing a complaint report with the NYPD or other law enforcement.
Provide information on counseling services available both on and off campus.
If a student, provide the complainant with the CUNY Student Bill of Rights (Appendix: A)
Advise the complainant of the CUNY Drug and Alcohol Use Amnesty Policy (Appendix B)
Supervisors: When complaints involving Title IX incidents occur, ensure that the following are completed:
Coordination with the Title IX Coordinator, Human Resources, Student Affairs;
Accompany complaint to a local hospital for initial medical services; and
Participate in interviews and disciplinary where appropriate.
CUNY Drug and Alcohol Use and Amnesty Policy
CUNY Equal Opportunity and Non-Discrimination Policy

The City University of New York Student Sexual Misconduct Complainants’ Bill of Rights CUNY students who experience campus-related sexual harassment or sexual violence, including sexual assault, stalking, domestic violence, intimate partner violence or dating violence, are entitled to the following rights:
To be provided with confidential on-campus counseling, and to be notified of other available services on- and off-campus.

To obtain, where appropriate, changes with respect to campus academic and living arrangements, no-contact orders, and other interim remedial measures to enable them to continue their education without undue stress or trauma.

To have their complaints handled respectfully by the campus, to be informed about how the campus will protect their privacy and confidentiality, and to have any allegations of retaliation addressed by the campus.
To file a criminal complaint and to seek an Order of Protection, with the assistance of the college, if they so choose.
To make a formal complaint at the campus as the first step in the disciplinary process against the respondent(s).

To have their complaint investigated in a prompt, impartial and thorough manner by individuals who have received appropriate training in conducting investigations and the issues related to sexual harassment and sexual violence.

To report incidents of sexual harassment or sexual violence that they experience while under the influence of alcohol or drugs without receiving discipline for their alcohol or drug use, if they agree to complete appropriate education or treatment as the circumstances warrant.

To have the same opportunity as the respondent(s) to participate in a student disciplinary hearing before a faculty-student disciplinary committee, including the right to be present, to be represented by a person of their choice, including an attorney, to present evidence, call witnesses, cross-examine witnesses, receive notice of the outcome of the hearing, and to appeal from the decision.
Questions about CUNY’s sexual misconduct policy and procedures may be directed to your campus Title IX Coordinator.

The City University of New York Drug/Alcohol Use Amnesty Policy The City University of New York’s (“CUNY’s”) Drug/Alcohol Use Amnesty Policy has two principal purposes. First, it is intended to encourage students to seek medical assistance related to drug and/or alcohol use without fear of being disciplined for such use. Because the use of drugs or alcohol may be life-threatening, CUNY wishes to reduce barriers to seeking and receiving medical help in those situations. Second, CUNY wishes to encourage students under the influence of drugs and/or alcohol who may be the victims of, witnesses to, or otherwise become aware of violence (including but not limited to domestic violence, dating violence, stalking, or sexual assault) or sexual harassment or gender-based harassment to report that violence or harassment. Toward that end, CUNY’s Policy is that students who seek medical assistance either for themselves or others and/or are reporting violence or harassment will not be subject to discipline under the circumstances described below.

Students who in good faith call for medical assistance for themselves or others and/or who receive medical assistance as a result of a call will not be disciplined for the consumption of alcohol (either if underage or if consumed in a CUNY-owned or operated residence hall or facility where alcohol consumption is prohibited) or drugs as long as there are no other violations that ordinarily would subject the student to disciplinary action. Similarly, studentswho may be the victims of, witnesses to, or otherwise become aware of violence or sexual harassment or gender-based harassment and who report such violence or harassment will not be disciplined for the consumption of alcohol or drugs in the absence of other violations that ordinarily would subject the student to disciplinary action. Other violations that would invoke discipline include but are not limited to (i) unlawful distribution of alcohol or drugs;(ii) sexual misconduct, as defined in CUNY’s Policy on Sexual Misconduct; (iii) causing or threatening physical harm; (iv) causing damage to property; (v) hazing.

The students involved will be encouraged to complete alcohol and/or drug education activities, assessment, and/or treatment, to be determined by the individual campuses or units of CUNY with which the students are affiliated. If repeated incidents of alcohol or drug use are involved, there may be issues of medical concern, which may result in parental notification, medical withdrawal, and/or other non-disciplinary responses.

CUNY’s Policy is intended both to implement Article 129-B of the Education Law (which mandates drug and alcohol amnesty for reporters of violence) and to complement New York State’s Good Samaritan Law, which is designed to encourage individuals to call 911 in the event of an alcohol or drug-related emergency. Generally, the Good Samaritan Law protects persons who witness or suffer from a medical emergency involving drugs or alcohol from being arrested or prosecuted for drug or underage alcohol possession after they call 911. It does not protect against arrest or prosecution for other offenses, such as the sale of drugs. Approved by the Board of Trustees on 6/30/2014, Cal. No. 7D and effective date of 7/1/2014 as ‘Medical Amnesty-Good Samaritan Policy’. Amended and changed to ‘Drug and Alcohol Use Amnesty Policy’ on 10/1/2015. Cal. No. 6D.

inst.title: Omniform System Access/Usage Policy
b: The City University of New York (CUNY) Department of Public Safety has entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the New York Police Department (NYPD) authorizing active CUNY Peace Officers access to the Omniform System in NYPD facilities to expedite the processing of arrests, aid in the detection, investigation and prevention of criminal activity, and to support law enforcement activities (see Appendix A).
The purpose of this instruction is to provide Members of the Service with guidance relative to the use and policies concerning access to the NYPD’s Omniform System.
Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) – An agreement between two or more parties which outlines the responsibilities of each of the parties to the agreement.

Omniform – A web-based graphical user interface (GUI) system incorporated into the NYPD's LAN system, facilitating complaint processing, arrest processing and supervisory functions at the precinct level.
As set forth in the Omniform System MOU the following conditions must be adhered to by all Members of the Service.

Each sworn member of the service will be trained in the use and policies of the Omniform System by the Public Safety Training Academy (PSTA) during their initial recruit training and in-service cycle as needed. Upon completion of initial training, officers will be required to sign a user agreement which acknowledges that he/she understands the usage constraints of the NYPD Omniform System and agrees to comply with these constraints (see Appendix B).

Each officer will be assigned a unique user identification and password to access the NYPD’s Omniform System by the NYPD’s Office of Information Technology and distributed by the PSTA. Officers are prohibited from sharing their assigned user credentials with any other person within or outside of the department.

Unauthorized use of the NYPD’s Omniform System can lead to disciplinary action and/or prosecution; under Section 156 of the New York State Penal Law. Section 156 of the New York State Penal Law includes § 156.05 Unauthorized use of a computer, a class A misdemeanor; § 156.10, Computer trespass, a class E felony, and § 156.30, Unlawful duplication of computer related material, a class E felony. The NYPD further reserves the right to prosecute under any other applicable section of the New York State Penal Law, or any other applicable law, rule or regulation.

It is the responsibility of each member of the service who has an account to access the Omniform System to maintain an active account. To ensure this process, each user must login to an authorized computer with access to the Omniform System in an NYPD facility within a 60-day period or call the NYPD helpdesk phone number (646) 610-6473 to reset a password prior to it being deactivated.

It is the responsibility of Public Safety Headquarters to make a prompt notification to the NYPD upon the resignation, termination, or other means of separation, of a member of the service who has been assigned user credentials to the Omniform System. To enable this process, campuses must make timely notifications to change in personnel.
Appendix A (NYPD–CUNY Omniform Memorandum of Understanding) and Appendix B (Omniform User Agreement) are not included here. Refer to the official Operations Guide.

inst.title: Tourniquet
b: The Department of Public Safety has distributed tourniquets to members of the SAFE Team as part of an officer safety and crisis response strategy that includes response to incidents where immediate care is needed to prevent loss of life. Tourniquets are designed to treat severe wounds to arms and legs with severe bleeding caused by gunshot wounds, auto accidents, and other injuries. The use of a tourniquet may be the best initial option to control severe extremity bleeding especially when a person has signs of hypovolemic shock (caused by blood loss), extremity injuries from explosive devices that result in the complete or nearly complete severing of limbs, in mass casualty situations, or when bleeding is profuse.

It is the policy of the Department of Public Safety that members of the service who are issued a tourniquet must complete an initial training on the use and care of the tourniquet and all the contents within the M-Fak. As part of this policy refresher training will be included as a segment during SAFE Team in-service cycles.
Tourniquet – A device for stopping the flow of blood through a vein or artery, typically by compressing a limb with a cord or tight bandage.
Training Assigned personnel will receive training in the use of a tourniquet. A review of this policy and the use of a tourniquet will be conducted during SAFE Team in- service cycles.

Deployment The tourniquet will be carried while on duty in the center line of the body, making it readily accessible by both hands. It will be brought to SAFE Team in-service Training, First Aid/CPR Training as well as Firearms Training if applicable.

Usage The tourniquet will be used in a manner consistent with the established training and as part of the overall sequence for treatment of hemorrhage control (Direct Pressure, Pressure Bandages etc.). All MOS must always follow universal precautions for blood-borne pathogens and refer to the training you received from the Public Safety Training Academy on First Aid, in addition to refresher training on your campus.

The CAT tourniquet can be applied in a one-handed or two-handed application. Place the tourniquet around the limb, it should be positioned as high as possible above the wound but not over a joint whenever possible.
One-Handed Application Insert the injured limb through the loop in the band and position the CAT two- three inches above the bleeding site directly to the skin.
Two-Handed Application Route the band around the limb, pass the red tip through the slit of the buckle, and position the Combat Application Tourniquet (CAT)

Pull band tightly and fasten it back on itself all the way around the limb, but not over the rod clips. Band should be tight enough that tips of three (3) fingers cannot be slid between the band and the limb. If the tips of three (3) fingers slide under band, retighten and re-secure.
between the band and the limb. If the tips of three (3) fingers slide under band, retighten and re-secure.
Twist the rod until bleeding has stopped.

Secure the rod inside a clip to lock it in place. Check for bleeding and distal pulse. If bleeding is not controlled, or distal pulse is present, consider additional tightening or applying a second CAT above and side-by-side to the first. Reassess.
Route the band between the clips and over the rod. Secure rod and band with TIME strap. Record time of application.

Note: If you cannot be sure or cannot take the additional time to examine where the bleeding is coming from based on the situation, the CAT can be effectively applied over clothing as high on the arm or leg as possible. The CAT must NOT be applied over solid objects within the clothing. As soon as the situation permits,
the injured limb should be evaluated and the CAT re-positioned 2”-3” above the injury directly to the skin.
Removal/Disposal of Tourniquet Once the tourniquet has been applied it should only be removed and disposed of by a doctor or physician from the hospital.
Maintenance/Replacement Each Member of the Service will be responsible for inspecting the kit assigned to him/her, for signs of damage and to ensure the kit has not expired.
If a kit is lost, damaged or has expired, the member shall report this to his/her supervisor and complete a University Incident report for a replacement.

Documentation/Notification The use of a tourniquet must be noted in the officer’s memo book and in a University Incident Report. In addition, notifications of the use of a tourniquet must be made in accordance to Operations Instruction #13.
Note: The use of a tourniquet other than the one issued by the University Department of Public Safety is permissible to prevent loss of life in extreme circumstances.

inst.title: Found Property Procedure
b: The Department of Public Safety’s receipt and handling of found property reflects upon the integrity of our department. The purpose of this procedure is to establish guidelines for the safekeeping, care, custody, and control of recovered property.
These procedures apply to all Public Safety employees when finding, receiving, processing, storing and disposing of found articles.
All members of the service (MOS) are required to safeguard found property and document when property is turned in to them at any and all times.
Upon receipt of found property the receiving MOS shall:
Notify the central dispatcher via landline or portable radio and give a description of said property to include the manner and location in which it was discovered.
Make an appropriate entry into his/her University Memo Book (UMB).

Await instructions from a supervisor or dispatcher which should include bringing the items to the Public Safety Office for further processing or transferring the items to another officer if the receiving officer is unable to return to the office.
Every time property changes hands both the giving and receiving MOS should make entries into their UMB.
Make appropriate entries into the command log and notify the tour supervisor.
Direct the actions of the MOS until the found item(s) are brought to the central command and properly vouchered.
Before the End of Tour, the Tour Supervisor must verify that all property vouchered during their tour is properly secured and a Found Item Report has been completed for each item.

MOS will bring the found property to the Public Safety Office and complete a Found Item Report in the university-wide reporting system. That same MOS will then print the voucher form and attach it to the found property (placed in evidence bag if possible) and the property will then be placed in a locked safe or secure storage facility located in the Public Safety Office.
Property that requires additional instruction are:

United States Currency (USC) amounting to over $100.00, illegal drugs, controlled substances, or contraband found on campus shall be vouchered at the NYPD precinct which includes the location in which the property was recovered. These actions shall be entered into a Found Item Report indicating the disposition of the property.

Recovered weapons shall only be handled by a sworn MOS. Firearms shall not be handled by MOS who have not received training in Firearms Safety. MOS who recover these items are to make an IMMEDIATE notification to the Central Dispatcher as well as requesting a Supervisor to the location.
Dispatchers: Upon being informed, should make an immediate notification to the NYPD.

Officers: Safeguard the area where the firearm is located to preserve the integrity of the scene and the found item. Upon the arrival of the NYPD the CUNY MOS will then follow the direction of the NYPD Supervisor regarding the vouchering process of firearm, ammunition, and other dangerous materials found.

Any dangerous or unlawful material vouchered require notifications as specified in Operations Instruction #13, Public Safety Notifications. Additionally, a Found Item Report indicating the disposition of the property is required.

Persons who report to Public Safety regarding the return of found property should be asked to describe the item(s) in question and to recount when the loss occurred. The servicing MOS should then conduct a check of the university-wide reporting system for a possible match of an item(s). The servicing MOS may conduct further questioning to verify that the person requesting the property is the rightful owner. If the property is to be turned over, the MOS must update the university- wide reporting system and print and complete a Property Release Form.
For sanitary reasons, the following items are not to be accepted into the Lost and Found: A. Food/drink and/or food/drink containers
Clothing items (including swimwear, socks, shoes, etc.)
Any items determined by a supervisor to be unsafe for storage (confer with Director or his/her designee)

If a rightful owner is identifiable based on the content of the recovered property, Public Safety shall make every effort to contact said individual. All attempts of contact shall be documented in the Found Item Report.
